lesson.title: Real Numbers: Filling In Every Gap on the Line
lesson.summary: The real numbers are exactly the numbers needed to fill in every point on the number line with no gaps, and their two key properties, completeness and density, are what make the idea of a limit possible in the first place.
lesson.body:
The number line looks solid, an unbroken line with no holes, but that impression only holds up if the numbers placed on it actually fill in every point. This is where the real numbers, denoted R, earn their name: they are exactly the numbers needed so that every point on the number line corresponds to a number, and every number corresponds to a point, with no gaps left over.

The real numbers also carry a strict order that behaves the way you would expect from the number line picture: for any two real numbers a and b, exactly one of three things is true, a < b, a = b, or a > b, a property called trichotomy. This order is also transitive (if a < b and b < c then a < c) and compatible with addition and with multiplication by positive numbers, which is why the same inequality rules used to solve for x also apply cleanly to real-valued limits and derivatives later on.

The real numbers split into two very different kinds. The rational numbers are ratios of integers, p/q with q not equal to 0, and include familiar values like 1/2, -7, and 0.333... (which equals 1/3). Written as decimals, rationals always either terminate or eventually repeat in a pattern. The irrational numbers are everything else on the line: numbers like pi, e, and sqrt(2), whose decimal expansions go on forever without ever settling into a repeating block. Both types are real numbers, and both are needed, because the rationals alone leave gaps.

Here is a classic way to see that sqrt(2) cannot be rational, so that a gap really would exist without irrationals. Suppose, for contradiction, that sqrt(2) = p/q where p and q are integers sharing no common factor. Squaring gives 2 = p^2/q^2, so p^2 = 2 q^2, which means p^2 is even, which forces p itself to be even (an odd number squared is always odd). Write p = 2k. Then (2k)^2 = 2 q^2 gives 4k^2 = 2 q^2, so q^2 = 2k^2, meaning q^2 is even, so q is even too. But then p and q share the factor 2, contradicting the assumption that they had no common factor. The contradiction means no such p/q exists: sqrt(2) is irrational, and the point on the number line at distance sqrt(2) from 0 is real but not rational.

A second key feature of the reals is density: between any two distinct real numbers, no matter how close together, there is always another real number, in fact infinitely many. For example, between 1.41 and 1.42 sits the rational number 1.415, and between 1.41 and 1.415 sits 1.4125, and this subdividing never runs out of room. This density is what makes it sensible to talk about a variable "approaching" a number by taking on values that get arbitrarily close, which is precisely the idea calculus is built on.

Together, completeness (no gaps) and density (no smallest step) are what make the real number line the right setting for limits. A function can only meaningfully get "closer and closer" to a value if there is an unbroken continuum of numbers to move through, and that continuum is exactly what the real numbers provide.
